justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, likely somewhere around 189–190. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the recent price with only a small directional bias, since short-term price action tends to mean-revert or continue momentum weakly. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to reflect a gentle bullish tilt, perhaps based on broader market trend or sector momentum. At the one-month horizon, I extended that drift a bit further, consistent with a modest positive expected return assumption over a longer window, though the incremental increase is deliberately small given how noisy equity prices are over that timeframe.

The confidence interval widths reflect the fundamental reality that price uncertainty compounds with time. At one day, typical daily volatility for an individual equity or ETF in the 190 range might be 1–2%, which maps roughly to the ±6.5 point band I used. At one week, volatility scales roughly with the square root of time, so I widened the band to about ±12–13 points. At one month, the interval expands to approximately ±25 points, capturing a broader range of plausible outcomes driven by earnings surprises, macro data releases, and shifts in risk sentiment over several weeks. These widths are calibrated to be fairly honest about how unpredictable short-to-medium term equity prices are.

There are several tail risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected negative earnings report, a sudden tightening in financial conditions, a geopolitical shock, or a broader equity market selloff could easily push prices 10–15% below my one-month estimate. On the upside, a blowout earnings beat, a surprise Federal Reserve pivot toward easier policy, or a sector-specific catalyst could drive prices sharply above the upper bound. Liquidity events or systemic market dislocations — the kinds of things that happen a few times per decade — are not fully captured in interval widths derived from normal volatility assumptions and represent genuine fat-tail risks at the one-month horizon especially.
